title: Game theory & oligopoly
examples: What is the difference between a monopoly and an oligopoly?
How does the payoff matrix help predict business behavior?
Can a company always find a Nash equilibrium?

explain.say: Today we learn about game theory in business. It helps predict choices when firms interact.

items: It models decisions made by multiple players.
Firms in an oligopoly are key players here.

explain.say: First we look at payoff matrices. These show the outcomes for each player.

items: Strategy A | Strategy B | Payoff (Player 1, Player 2)
Strategy C | Strategy D | Payoff (Player 1, Player 2)

explain.say: A payoff matrix uses numbers to show gains or losses. Each number pair is an outcome.
Next we find the dominant strategy. This is the best move regardless of what others do.
The Nash equilibrium is a stable outcome. No player wants to change their strategy alone.

draw.text: Nash Equilibrium: No Incentive to Change

explain.say: In the real world, consider two competing coffee shops. They must set prices. Their choices form a game.

faq.q: What is the difference between a dominant strategy and Nash equilibrium?
faq.a: A dominant strategy is the best move for one player no matter what others do. The Nash equilibrium is a set of strategies where no single player can improve their outcome by changing alone.

faq.q: Does the payoff matrix always show all possible outcomes?
faq.a: Yes, the matrix must account for every combination of strategies available to all involved players. If an outcome is missing, the analysis is incomplete.
asks: How many cells are in a 3-player matrix?
Can I skip some outcomes in the matrix?

faq.q: What does a payoff of (5, 10) mean for two companies?
faq.a: It means the first company gets a payoff of five, and the second company gets a payoff of ten. The numbers correspond to the order of the players.

faq.q: Can I use game theory for things other than business?
faq.a: Yes, it is used in biology to model predator-prey relationships. It can also be used in political science to model voting behavior.

faq.q: If there is no dominant strategy, can I still find a Nash equilibrium?
faq.a: Yes, finding a Nash equilibrium is possible even without a single dominant strategy for every player. The equilibrium relies on mutual best responses.
asks: What if the game is zero-sum?
Does the absence of dominance mean no equilibrium?

facts: Oligopoly describes a market with few large sellers.
The payoff matrix organizes outcomes into pairs of numbers.
A dominant strategy yields the best payoff regardless of rivals' actions.
The Nash equilibrium represents a stable state where no player benefits from unilateral deviation.

quiz.say: If Player A always gets a higher payoff by choosing Option X, regardless of what Player B chooses, what is this strategy?
quiz.why: It is the best choice for Player A in every scenario.

wrong.1: This is a specific stable outcome, not a universal best move.
wrong.2: This only describes the best move against one specific choice.
wrong.3: This term is too general and lacks the specific comparison needed.

quiz.say: In a payoff matrix, if the payoffs are (5, 10), who receives the payoff of ten?
quiz.why: The payoff order listed is typically (Player 1, Player 2).

wrong.1: The first number always belongs to the first player listed.
wrong.2: The structure of the matrix dictates which number belongs to whom.
wrong.3: The number's value does not determine which player it belongs to.

quiz.say: If both companies choose the 'Low Price' option, and the payoffs are (3, 3), what does this suggest about the market?

options.show: It means both companies are losing money.
options.say: It means both companies are losing money.

options.show: It means one company dominates the other.
options.say: It means one company dominates the other.

options.show: It is a potential Nash Equilibrium.
options.say: It is a potential Nash Equilibrium.

quiz.why: Neither company wants to unilaterally change their price because the other player would also change theirs.

wrong.0: The payoff is just a relative measure of gain or loss, not absolute profit.
wrong.1: A balanced equilibrium suggests mutual stability, not dominance.
wrong.3: Game theory shows possibilities, not certainties in the real world.
